claim: Chx10-labeled V2a neurons are divided into at least two morphological subtypes proposed to play distinct roles in timing and intensity control.
source: Chx10-labeled V2a neurons are divided into at least two morphological subtypes proposed to play distinct roles in timing and intensity control.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by references to prior work and the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Descending V2a subtypes are recruited exclusively at slow or fast speeds.
source: Consistent with distinct rhythm generating and output patterning functions within the spinal V2a population, we find that descending subtypes are recruited exclusively at slow or fast speeds and exhibit intrinsic cellular properties suitable for rhythmogenesis at those speeds, while bifurcating subtypes are recruited more reliably at all speeds and lack appropriate rhythmogenic cellular properties.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2-4.

claim: Descending V2a subtypes exhibit intrinsic cellular properties suitable for rhythmogenesis at slow or fast speeds.
source: Consistent with distinct rhythm generating and output patterning functions within the spinal V2a population, we find that descending subtypes are recruited exclusively at slow or fast speeds and exhibit intrinsic cellular properties suitable for rhythmogenesis at those speeds, while bifurcating subtypes are recruited more reliably at all speeds and lack appropriate rhythmogenic cellular properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by current-clamp recordings showing bursting and tonic firing properties in descending V2a neurons that match swim frequencies (Figure 2).

claim: Bifurcating V2a subtypes are recruited more reliably at all speeds.
source: Consistent with distinct rhythm generating and output patterning functions within the spinal V2a population, we find that descending subtypes are recruited exclusively at slow or fast speeds and exhibit intrinsic cellular properties suitable for rhythmogenesis at those speeds, while bifurcating subtypes are recruited more reliably at all speeds and lack appropriate rhythmogenic cellular properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell-attached recordings showing higher recruitment probabilities across frequencies (Figures 3-4).

claim: Bifurcating V2a subtypes lack appropriate rhythmogenic cellular properties.
source: Consistent with distinct rhythm generating and output patterning functions within the spinal V2a population, we find that descending subtypes are recruited exclusively at slow or fast speeds and exhibit intrinsic cellular properties suitable for rhythmogenesis at those speeds, while bifurcating subtypes are recruited more reliably at all speeds and lack appropriate rhythmogenic cellular properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by current-clamp data showing that chattering and bursting properties in bifurcating V2a neurons do not match their swim-firing patterns (Figure 2).

claim: At fast speeds reciprocal inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing.
source: Unexpectedly, however, phasic firing patterns during locomotion in rhythmogenic and non-rhythmogenic V2a neurons alike are best explained by distinct modes of synaptic inhibition linked to cell type and speed. At fast speeds reciprocal inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing, while recurrent inhibition in bifurcating V2a neurons helps pattern motor output.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by voltage-clamp recordings showing anti-phase inhibition in fast descending V2a neurons (Figure 6).

claim: At fast speeds recurrent inhibition in bifurcating V2a neurons helps pattern motor output.
source: At fast speeds reciprocal inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing, while recurrent inhibition in bifurcating V2a neurons helps pattern motor output.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by voltage-clamp recordings showing in-phase inhibition in fast bifurcating V2a neurons (Figure 6).

claim: At slow speeds recurrent inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing.
source: In contrast, at slow speeds recurrent inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing, while bifurcating V2a neurons rely on reciprocal inhibition alone to pattern output.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by voltage-clamp recordings showing in-phase inhibition in slow descending V2a neurons (Figure 6).

claim: At slow speeds bifurcating V2a neurons rely on reciprocal inhibition alone to pattern output.
source: In contrast, at slow speeds recurrent inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing, while bifurcating V2a neurons rely on reciprocal inhibition alone to pattern output.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by voltage-clamp recordings showing predominantly anti-phase inhibition in slow bifurcating V2a neurons (Figure 6).

claim: Cell-type-specific, not common, modes of rhythmogenesis generate and coordinate different speeds of locomotion.
source: Our findings suggest cell-type-specific, not common, modes of rhythmogenesis generate and coordinate different speeds of locomotion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing all experimental findings.

claim: All forms of vertebrate locomotion rely on rhythmic activity in muscles operating as functional antagonists.
source: All forms of vertebrate locomotion rely on rhythmic activity in muscles operating as functional antagonists (Grillner, 1985).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Swimming in fishes relies on left–right alternation of axial muscles across the body.
source: For instance, swimming in fishes relies on left–right alternation of axial muscles across the body, while walking in mammals relies on flexor–extensor alternation along it.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about fish locomotion.

claim: Walking in mammals relies on flexor–extensor alternation along the body.
source: For instance, swimming in fishes relies on left–right alternation of axial muscles across the body, while walking in mammals relies on flexor–extensor alternation along it.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about mammalian locomotion.

claim: A landmark hypothesis posed over a century ago argued for corresponding excitatory 'half-centers' within spinal cord with reciprocal, feedforward inhibition between half-centers generating rhythmic output.
source: A landmark hypothesis posed over a century ago argued for corresponding excitatory 'half-centers' within spinal cord (e.g., left–right or flexor–extensor), with reciprocal, feedforward inhibition between half-centers generating rhythmic output (Brown, 1911).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citation to Brown, 1911.

claim: Reciprocal inhibition has been relegated to patterning activity between so-called 'unit burst generators' capable of rhythmogenesis via recurrent, feedback excitatory connections.
source: Since then reciprocal inhibition has been relegated to patterning activity between so-called 'unit burst generators' capable of rhythmogenesis via recurrent, feedback excitatory connections (Grillner and Kozlov, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about current theory supported by citation.

claim: Simulations adjusting the synaptic coupling strength between segmental axial unit burst generators can explain changes in the speed and direction of swimming in lampreys.
source: For example, simulations adjusting the synaptic coupling strength between segmental axial unit burst generators can explain changes in the speed and direction of swimming in lampreys (Kozlov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claim: Simulations altering the synaptic coupling between segmental limb unit burst generators can replicate different speeds and gaits of locomotion in cats.
source: Likewise, simulations altering the synaptic coupling between segmental limb unit burst generators can replicate different speeds and gaits of locomotion in cats (Grillner, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claim: Another theory explaining speed-dependent changes in coordination stratifies 'rhythm' and 'pattern' control.
source: Another theory explaining speed-dependent changes in coordination stratifies 'rhythm' and 'pattern' control (Perret and Cabelguen, 1980; Koshland and Smith, 1989; Kriellaars et al., 1994; Burke et al., 2001; Lafreniere-Roula and McCrea, 2005), where populations of interneurons generating higher- or lower-frequency rhythms feed into separate populations coordinating distinct patterns of motor output (McCrea and Rybak, 2008; Ausborn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by multiple citations.

claim: Studies in zebrafish and mice suggest separate spinal populations are active at different locomotor speeds with distinct patterns of motor output.
source: In support, studies in zebrafish and mice suggest separate spinal populations are active at different locomotor speeds with distinct patterns of motor output (McLean et al., 2008; Talpalar et al., 2013; Satou et al., 2020; Picton et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Rhythmogenesis is presumed to originate from a common mechanism regardless of speed, reliant on cellular properties or synaptic drive or both.
source: Critically, however, rhythmogenesis is presumed to originate from a common mechanism regardless of speed, reliant on cellular properties or synaptic drive or both (Guertin, 2009; Brocard et al., 2010; Ryczko et al., 2010; Ziskind-Conhaim and Hochman, 2017; El Manira, 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about prevailing assumptions in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Larval zebrafish generate two basic modes of forward swimming or 'gaits'.
source: Like all fish, larval zebrafish generate two basic modes of forward swimming or 'gaits' (Di Santo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about zebrafish locomotion supported by citation.

claim: Anguilliform mode is typically reserved for escaping predators and uses higher-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the trunk.
source: Anguilliform mode is typically reserved for escaping predators and uses higher-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the trunk, while carangiform mode utilizes lower-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the tail for exploration and pursuing prey (Budick and O'Malley, 2000; Müller and van Leeuwen, 2004; Thorsen et al., 2004; Patterson et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a characterization of zebrafish swimming modes supported by multiple citations.

claim: Carangiform mode utilizes lower-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the tail for exploration and pursuing prey.
source: Anguilliform mode is typically reserved for escaping predators and uses higher-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the trunk, while carangiform mode utilizes lower-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the tail for exploration and pursuing prey (Budick and O'Malley, 2000; Müller and van Leeuwen, 2004; Thorsen et al., 2004; Patterson et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a characterization of zebrafish swimming modes supported by multiple citations.

claim: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order.
source: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order (Myers et al., 1986), size (McLean et al., 2007), relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers (Bello-Rojas et al., 2019), and molecular signatures (D'Elia et al., 2023; Pallucchi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing motor neuron properties.

claim: Axial motor neurons are distinguished by size.
source: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order (Myers et al., 1986), size (McLean et al., 2007), relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers (Bello-Rojas et al., 2019), and molecular signatures (D'Elia et al., 2023; Pallucchi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McLean et al., 2007.

claim: Axial motor neurons are distinguished by relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers.
source: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order (Myers et al., 1986), size (McLean et al., 2007), relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers (Bello-Rojas et al., 2019), and molecular signatures (D'Elia et al., 2023; Pallucchi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bello-Rojas et al., 2019.

claim: Axial motor neurons are distinguished by molecular signatures.
source: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order (Myers et al., 1986), size (McLean et al., 2007), relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers (Bello-Rojas et al., 2019), and molecular signatures (D'Elia et al., 2023; Pallucchi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Elia et al., 2023 and Pallucchi et al., 2024.

claim: Current- and voltage-clamp recordings from motor neurons have revealed differences in rhythmogenic cellular properties and synaptic drive between the different types.
source: Current- and voltage-clamp recordings from motor neurons have revealed differences in rhythmogenic cellular properties and synaptic drive between the different types (Menelaou and McLean, 2012; Kishore et al., 2014), suggesting different forms of rhythmogenesis could be responsible for different speeds of locomotion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the same lab.

claim: Chx10-labeled spinal V2a interneurons provide a major source of phasic premotor excitation during locomotion in zebrafish and mice.
source: To test this idea, we performed current- and voltage-clamp recordings from Chx10-labeled spinal V2a interneurons, which provide a major source of phasic premotor excitation during locomotion in zebrafish and mice (McLean and Dougherty, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Morphologically distinct V2a neurons sort into rhythm-generating and pattern-forming subtypes based on distinct cellular properties linked to distinct patterns of recruitment and synaptic drive.
source: We find that morphologically distinct V2a neurons sort into rhythm-generating and pattern-forming subtypes based on distinct cellular properties linked to distinct patterns of recruitment and synaptic drive.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the Introduction and supported by data in Figures 2-6.

claim: Among descending V2a neurons that qualify as rhythm-generating, reciprocal inhibition originating from contralateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at fast speeds.
source: Critically, among descending V2a neurons that qualify as rhythm-generating, reciprocal inhibition originating from contralateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at fast speeds, while recurrent inhibition from ipsilateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at slow speeds.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claim: Among descending V2a neurons that qualify as rhythm-generating, recurrent inhibition from ipsilateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at slow speeds.
source: Critically, among descending V2a neurons that qualify as rhythm-generating, reciprocal inhibition originating from contralateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at fast speeds, while recurrent inhibition from ipsilateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at slow speeds.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claim: For bifurcating V2a neurons considered pattern-forming, recurrent inhibition supports phasic firing at fast speeds.
source: For bifurcating V2a neurons considered pattern-forming, the opposite is true – recurrent inhibition supports phasic firing at fast speeds and reciprocal inhibition at slow speeds.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claim: For bifurcating V2a neurons considered pattern-forming, reciprocal inhibition supports phasic firing at slow speeds.
source: For bifurcating V2a neurons considered pattern-forming, the opposite is true – recurrent inhibition supports phasic firing at fast speeds and reciprocal inhibition at slow speeds.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claim: V2a neurons are organized into fast and slow subtypes based on dorsoventral (DV) soma position and birth order.
source: From our previous work studying V2a neurons in larval zebrafish we know they are organized into: (1) fast and slow subtypes based on dorsoventral (DV) soma position and birth order (McLean et al., 2007; McLean et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009), and (2) distinct subtypes that provide stronger direct versus indirect control of motor neuron recruitment (Menelaou et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the same lab.

claim: V2a neurons with descending axons (V2a-D) provide stronger inputs to other premotor interneurons.
source: Specifically, V2a neurons with descending axons (V2a-D) provide stronger inputs to other premotor interneurons, while V2a neurons with bifurcating axons (V2a-B) provide stronger inputs to motor neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), in line with differential rhythm and pattern control.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: V2a neurons with bifurcating axons (V2a-B) provide stronger inputs to motor neurons.
source: Specifically, V2a neurons with descending axons (V2a-D) provide stronger inputs to other premotor interneurons, while V2a neurons with bifurcating axons (V2a-B) provide stronger inputs to motor neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), in line with differential rhythm and pattern control.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Midbody V2a neurons would be recruited during both fast anguilliform and slow carangiform modes.
source: To record from distinct types of V2a neurons, we targeted green fluorescent protein (GFP)-positive neurons located at midbody in the Tg(Chx10:GFP) line (Figure 1A, B; Kimura et al., 2006), since midbody neurons would be recruited during both fast anguilliform and slow carangiform modes (Müller and van Leeuwen, 2004; Thorsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of zebrafish swimming.

claim: V2a-D and V2a-B neurons recruited at fast speeds can be distinguished by levels of Chx10 expression in transgenic lines.
source: V2a-D and V2a-B neurons recruited at fast speeds can be distinguished by levels of Chx10 expression in transgenic lines (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), as reported in mice (Hayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in zebrafish and mice.

claim: Larger, dimmer V2a neurons intermingled with smaller, brighter neurons along the DV axis.
source: Larger, dimmer V2a neurons intermingled with smaller, brighter neurons along the DV axis (Figure 1C, left), but occupied more lateral positions (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Larger, dimmer V2a neurons occupied more lateral positions than smaller, brighter neurons.
source: Larger, dimmer V2a neurons intermingled with smaller, brighter neurons along the DV axis (Figure 1C, left), but occupied more lateral positions (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is no significant difference in DV distribution between low and high GFP-positive V2a neuron types.
source: Statistical analysis confirmed these observations, with no significant difference in either DV distribution (Figure 1D, left) or number per segment between the low or high GFP-positive types (Figure 1D, right), but a significant difference in ML position (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D with statistical test results.

claim: There is no significant difference in number per segment between low and high GFP-positive V2a neuron types.
source: Statistical analysis confirmed these observations, with no significant difference in either DV distribution (Figure 1D, left) or number per segment between the low or high GFP-positive types (Figure 1D, right), but a significant difference in ML position (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D with statistical test results.

claim: There is a significant difference in ML position between low and high GFP-positive V2a neuron types.
source: Statistical analysis confirmed these observations, with no significant difference in either DV distribution (Figure 1D, left) or number per segment between the low or high GFP-positive types (Figure 1D, right), but a significant difference in ML position (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E with statistical test results.

claim: During real swimming escape responses decelerate, beginning in fast anguilliform mode and ending in slow carangiform mode.
source: During real swimming escape responses decelerate (Video 1), beginning in fast anguilliform mode and ending in slow carangiform mode (McLean et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text, supported by citations, and illustrated in Video 1.

claim: Plots of ventral rootlet burst frequencies with time confirm the deceleration pattern during 'fictive' escape responses.
source: Plots of ventral rootlet burst frequencies with time confirm this pattern during 'fictive' escape responses, where we observe the highest frequencies at the beginning of the swim episode immediately following the stimulus (Figure 1G, left).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Zebrafish swimming is episodic.
source: Notably, zebrafish swimming is episodic (McHenry and Lauder, 2006; Soto and McHenry, 2020) and so it can continue intermittently after the initial escape swim episode.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Subsequent swim episodes (Swim 2+) rarely exceeded peak firing frequencies observed in the first stimulus-evoked episode (>60 Hz in Swim 1).
source: Subsequent episodes (Swim 2+) rarely exceeded peak firing frequencies observed in the first stimulus-evoked episode (>60 Hz in Swim 1) and there was more variability in frequency (Figure 1G, right).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: All high GFP neurons targeted for recordings were V2a-Ds.
source: By including dye in our recording pipette, we confirmed post hoc that all high GFP neurons we targeted for recordings were V2a-Ds and all low GFP neurons were V2a-Bs (Figure 2A), as we would expect based on our prior work (Menelaou and McLean, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2A, and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: All low GFP neurons targeted for recordings were V2a-Bs.
source: By including dye in our recording pipette, we confirmed post hoc that all high GFP neurons we targeted for recordings were V2a-Ds and all low GFP neurons were V2a-Bs (Figure 2A), as we would expect based on our prior work (Menelaou and McLean, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2A, and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Differences in sizes and DV distributions of V2a-D and V2a-B neurons in the current-clamp dataset were consistent with analysis of high and low GFP neurons in stable lines.
source: Differences in sizes and DV distributions of V2a-D and V2a-B neurons in our current-clamp dataset (n = 47) were consistent with our analysis of high and low GFP neurons in stable lines (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Measurements of input resistance and rheobase current were consistent with differences in sizes and excitability between V2a-D and V2a-B types.
source: Also, measurements of input resistance and rheobase current were consistent with differences in sizes and excitability between the two types (Figure 2C, left).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: V2a-D neurons with 'tonic' responses were distributed dorsally and had the lowest input resistances in their respective types.
source: V2a-D neurons with 'tonic' responses and V2a-B neurons with higher-frequency 'chattering' ones were distributed dorsally and had the lowest input resistances in their respective types (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2B-E.

claim: V2a-B neurons with higher-frequency 'chattering' responses were distributed dorsally and had the lowest input resistances in their respective types.
source: V2a-D neurons with 'tonic' responses and V2a-B neurons with higher-frequency 'chattering' ones were distributed dorsally and had the lowest input resistances in their respective types (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2B-E.

claim: In tonic V2a-Ds, firing above rheobase current was observed consistently throughout the current step.
source: In tonic V2a-Ds, firing above rheobase current was observed consistently throughout the current step (Figure 2E, top), with instantaneous spike rates increasing linearly with increasing current, starting around 40 Hz and reaching 200 Hz (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: In tonic V2a-Ds, instantaneous spike rates increased linearly with increasing current, starting around 40 Hz and reaching 200 Hz.
source: In tonic V2a-Ds, firing above rheobase current was observed consistently throughout the current step (Figure 2E, top), with instantaneous spike rates increasing linearly with increasing current, starting around 40 Hz and reaching 200 Hz (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In chattering V2a-Bs, firing above rheobase current was intermittent throughout the step.
source: In chattering V2a-Bs, firing above rheobase current was intermittent throughout the step (Figure 2F, top), with instantaneous rates starting around 200 Hz and reaching 600 Hz (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D and 2F.

claim: In chattering V2a-Bs, instantaneous rates started around 200 Hz and reached 600 Hz.
source: In chattering V2a-Bs, firing above rheobase current was intermittent throughout the step (Figure 2F, top), with instantaneous rates starting around 200 Hz and reaching 600 Hz (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Observations of tonic V2a-D and chattering V2a-B firing patterns are consistent with previous recordings from fast V2a-D and V2a-B neurons.
source: These observations are consistent with previous recordings from fast V2a-D and V2a-B neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: V2a-D and V2a-B neurons with 'burst' responses were distributed ventrally and had the highest input resistances within their respective types.
source: On the other hand, V2a-D and V2a-B neurons with 'burst' responses were distributed ventrally and had the highest input resistances within their respective types (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2B-E.

claim: In bursting V2a neurons, firing above rheobase was characterized by higher-frequency spikes superimposed on lower-frequency membrane potential oscillations.
source: In bursting V2a neurons, firing above rheobase was characterized by higher-frequency spikes superimposed on lower-frequency membrane potential oscillations (Figure 2E, F, bottom).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: The frequency of the slower oscillations in bursting V2a neurons increased with current.
source: While the frequency of the slower oscillations increased with current (Figure 2E, F, bottom), instantaneous spike rates were already close to peak values at rheobase (500–600 Hz; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D, 2E, and 2F.

claim: Instantaneous spike rates in bursting V2a neurons were already close to peak values at rheobase (500–600 Hz).
source: While the frequency of the slower oscillations increased with current (Figure 2E, F, bottom), instantaneous spike rates were already close to peak values at rheobase (500–600 Hz; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Beyond 2–3x rheobase current, slower oscillations in bursting V2a neurons were no longer obvious and the firing pattern more closely resembled the chattering one.
source: Beyond 2–3x rheobase current, slower oscillations were no longer obvious and the firing pattern more closely resembled the chattering one (data not shown), as observed previously for motor neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to prior work on motor neurons.

claim: Tonic V2a-D and chattering V2a-B neurons were recruited at the beginning of the episode at median swim frequencies above 30 Hz.
source: As expected (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), both tonic V2a-D and chattering V2a-B neurons were recruited at the beginning of the episode at median swim frequencies above 30 Hz (Figure 2G, H), consistent with recruitment during fast anguilliform mode (Thorsen et al., 2004; McLean et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figures 2G and 2H, and supported by citations.

claim: Burst V2a-Ds fired more reliably at the end of the episode at median frequencies that rarely exceeded 30 Hz.
source: In contrast, burst V2a-Ds fired more reliably at the end of the episode at median frequencies that rarely exceeded 30 Hz (Figure 2G, H), consistent with participation in slow carangiform mode (Thorsen et al., 2004; McLean et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figures 2G and 2H, and supported by citations.

claim: Burst V2a-Bs were recruited just below 30 Hz, and fired more reliably throughout the episode and over a broader frequency range.
source: Burst V2a-Bs were recruited just below 30 Hz, and fired more reliably throughout the episode and over a broader frequency range (Figure 2G, H), particularly compared to the narrow range of bursting V2a-Ds (two sample Kolmogrov–Smirnov test on density distributions; D = 0.157, p < 0.001; BB, n = 6, BD, n = 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figures 2G and 2H, and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A comparison between the step- and swim-firing patterns among V2a-D neurons revealed a remarkable correspondence.
source: A comparison between the step- and swim-firing patterns among V2a-D neurons revealed a remarkable correspondence (Figure 2G), with median spike frequencies (tonic) or oscillation frequencies (burst) overlapping median recruitment frequencies during swimming (Figure 2I, left).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2G and 2I.

claim: Median spike frequencies (tonic) or oscillation frequencies (burst) in V2a-D neurons overlap median recruitment frequencies during swimming.
source: A comparison between the step- and swim-firing patterns among V2a-D neurons revealed a remarkable correspondence (Figure 2G), with median spike frequencies (tonic) or oscillation frequencies (burst) overlapping median recruitment frequencies during swimming (Figure 2I, left).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The link between step- and swim-firing patterns was less obvious for V2a-B neurons.
source: However, the link between step- and swim-firing patterns was less obvious for V2a-B neurons (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: While bursting V2a-B neurons recruited at swim frequencies exceeding 60 Hz had higher-frequency oscillations, step bursting rarely exceeded 20 Hz.
source: For example, while bursting V2a-B neurons recruited at swim frequencies exceeding 60 Hz had higher-frequency oscillations, step bursting rarely exceeded 20 Hz (Figure 2I, right).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: For chattering V2a-B neurons, there were no clear subthreshold oscillations to calculate rhythmicity.
source: For chattering V2a-B neurons, there were no clear subthreshold oscillations to calculate rhythmicity and the broad range of spike frequencies resulted in large standard deviations (±74–130 Hz, n = 5) that rendered median values less interpretable.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the analysis of chattering V2a-B neurons.

claim: Distinct electrophysiological properties define distinct V2a types recruited at different speeds.
source: Thus, distinct electrophysiological properties define distinct V2a types recruited at different speeds and V2a-D neurons are better suited to providing intrinsic rhythmogenic activity during fast and slow swimming modes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the current-clamp data presented.

claim: V2a-D neurons are better suited to providing intrinsic rhythmogenic activity during fast and slow swimming modes.
source: Thus, distinct electrophysiological properties define distinct V2a types recruited at different speeds and V2a-D neurons are better suited to providing intrinsic rhythmogenic activity during fast and slow swimming modes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the current-clamp data showing correspondence between intrinsic and swim firing patterns in V2a-D neurons.

claim: V2a-B neurons rely more on rhythmic synaptic drive to shape their phasic firing patterns during swimming.
source: This is consistent with their proposed rhythm-generating and pattern-forming roles (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), and suggests V2a-B neurons rely more on rhythmic synaptic drive to shape their phasic firing patterns during swimming.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correspondence between step- and swim-firing patterns in V2a-B neurons.

claim: V2a-D and V2a-B neurons that fired at the beginning of the escape episode or nearer the end were found in the voltage-clamp dataset.
source: Consistent with our current-clamp recordings, in our voltage-clamp dataset (n = 39) we found V2a-D and V2a-B neurons that fired at the beginning of the escape episode or nearer the end (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: V2a-D neurons fired more sparsely than V2a-B neurons.
source: V2a-D neurons fired more sparsely (Figure 3A, left) and were divided into two distinct groups: (1) neurons that fired exclusively at the beginning of the episode at median swim frequencies exceeding 40 Hz, and (2) neurons that fired later on in the episode at median swim frequencies rarely exceeding 30 Hz (Figure 3B, top and bottom left; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: V2a-D neurons were divided into two distinct groups based on firing timing and frequency.

source: In larval zebrafish, there are two 'gaits' during forward swimming as defined by limb coordination – slow carangiform mode which involves cyclical abduction/adduction of pectoral fins that alternates across the body and fast anguilliform mode which involves bilateral fin adduction (Thorsen et al., 2004).

source: The transition in fin coordination occurs abruptly between tail beat frequencies of 30–40 Hz in larvae, with graded increases in the cyclical frequency and intensity of body bends leading to increased yaw displacement of the head at faster speeds (Thorsen et al., 2004; McLean et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

source: Notwithstanding differences in cellular ablation versus synaptic silencing approaches and their relative sensitivity to potential compensatory mechanisms (Schnerwitzki et al., 2018; Del Pozo et al., 2020), our strategy also included dI6 neurons that extended into the hindbrain (Figure 7A, arrow).

claim: Reciprocal inhibition nearer the hindbrain/spinal cord is essential for generating high-frequency rhythms.
source: By subtractive reasoning, this argues that reciprocal inhibition nearer the hindbrain/spinal cord is essential for generating high-frequency rhythms.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the current results to prior ablation studies.

source: In zebrafish and mice (Hayashi et al., 2018; Menelaou and McLean, 2019), V2a neurons have been categorized into descending (I) and bifurcating (II) subtypes (Figure 8A, top).

claim: Type I and II V2a neurons in larval zebrafish differ in axon trajectories, rostro-caudal distribution, size, Chx10 levels, connectivity, and ML distribution in the spinal cord.
source: Our data only strengthen cross-species links by demonstrating that type I and II V2a neurons in larval zebrafish not only differ in axon trajectories, rostro-caudal distribution, size, Chx10 levels, and connectivity, but also in their ML distribution in the spinal cord (Figure 1C).

claim: In zebrafish, there are at least two potential sources of ipsilateral inhibition, V1 neurons and V2b neurons.
source: In zebrafish, as in mice, there are at least two potential sources of ipsilateral inhibition, V1 neurons (Higashijima et al., 2004) and V2b neurons (Callahan et al., 2019), and two potential sources of commissural inhibition (Satou et al., 2020), dI6 neurons and V0d neurons (Figure 8A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 8A.

source: In zebrafish, as in mice, there are at least two potential sources of ipsilateral inhibition, V1 neurons (Higashijima et al., 2004) and V2b neurons (Callahan et al., 2019), and two potential sources of commissural inhibition (Satou et al., 2020), dI6 neurons and V0d neurons (Figure 8A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: Cell-attached and voltage-clamp data support distinct slow and fast type I V2a-Ds defined by selective within module connectivity.
source: Consistent with this idea, our cell-attached and voltage-clamp data support distinct slow and fast type I V2a-Ds defined by selective within module connectivity.

claim: Type I V2a neurons converge on slow and fast type II V2a-Bs, which relay integrated frequency information to their respective motor pools.
source: These neurons in turn converge on slow and fast type II V2a-Bs, which relay integrated frequency information to their respective motor pools (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: In the fast module, rhythmogenesis orchestrated by type I V2a neurons relies on reciprocal inhibition.
source: In the fast module, rhythmogenesis orchestrated by type I V2a neurons relies on reciprocal inhibition.

claim: Cell-type-specific optical ablation and silencing studies in adult lampreys suggest reciprocal inhibition is essential for rhythmogenesis during anguilliform swimming.
source: This is consistent with cell-type-specific optical ablation and silencing studies in adult lampreys (Buchanan and McPherson, 1995) and embryonic frogs (Moult et al., 2013) that suggest reciprocal inhibition is essential for rhythmogenesis during anguilliform swimming.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in other species.

claim: Cell-type-specific optical ablation and silencing studies in embryonic frogs suggest reciprocal inhibition is essential for rhythmogenesis during anguilliform swimming.
source: This is consistent with cell-type-specific optical ablation and silencing studies in adult lampreys (Buchanan and McPherson, 1995) and embryonic frogs (Moult et al., 2013) that suggest reciprocal inhibition is essential for rhythmogenesis during anguilliform swimming.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in other species.

claim: Rhythmic activity can be generated in surgically isolated hemi-cords and surgically divided spinal cords of lampreys and frog embryos.
source: Rhythmic activity can also be generated in surgically isolated hemi-cords and surgically divided spinal cords of lampreys and frog embryos (Kahn and Roberts, 1982; Soffe, 1989; Cangiano and Grillner, 2003; Cangiano and Grillner, 2005; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the fast module, recurrent inhibition helps limit motor output via type II V2a-Bs.
source: In the fast module, recurrent inhibition helps limit motor output via type II V2a-Bs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Type II V2a-Bs have relatively strong connections to motor neurons.
source: Type II V2a-Bs have relatively strong connections to motor neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), so limiting their firing would ensure that motor output does not exceed 50% of the duty cycle and risk bilateral co-contraction as the interval between cyclical bursts decreases with increased speed (Grillner, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the slow module, recurrent inhibition is more obvious in type I V2a-D neurons.
source: On the other hand, the cell-type-dependent dominance of reciprocal versus recurrent inhibition is flipped when considering the slow module. Instead, recurrent inhibition is more obvious in type I V2a-D neurons, while type II V2a-B neurons rely exclusively on reciprocal inhibition to pattern their activity (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: In the slow module, type II V2a-B neurons rely exclusively on reciprocal inhibition to pattern their activity.
source: On the other hand, the cell-type-dependent dominance of reciprocal versus recurrent inhibition is flipped when considering the slow module. Instead, recurrent inhibition is more obvious in type I V2a-D neurons, while type II V2a-B neurons rely exclusively on reciprocal inhibition to pattern their activity (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: Until now recurrent inhibition was linked to limiting motor output, not to rhythmogenesis.
source: Until now recurrent inhibition was linked to limiting motor output (Hultborn et al., 1979), not to rhythmogenesis (see, however, Lindén and Berg, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During somatosensory-evoked swimming, type I and II V2a neurons fire more synchronously than during visually evoked swimming.
source: Thus, it appears that during somatosensory-evoked swimming, where intensity and frequency are coupled over a broad range of speeds, type I and II V2a neurons fire more synchronously than during visually evoked swimming, where intensity and frequency are uncoupled over a more narrow speed range.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the current data to prior work on optomotor responses.

claim: Recent work has identified promising molecular markers that distinguish slow and fast type I and II V2a neurons.
source: While this highlights the modular nature of timing (rhythm) and intensity (pattern) control within the spinal V2a population, future experiments testing this idea will rely on identifying molecular markers that distinguish slow and fast type I and II V2a neurons. Fortunately, recent work has identified promising candidates (Pallucchi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: In juvenile/adult zebrafish, V2a and motor neurons have been grouped into slow, intermediate, fast, and escape modules based on patterns of recruitment and phasic synaptic drive during fictive swimming.
source: In juvenile/adult zebrafish, V2a and motor neurons have been grouped into slow, intermediate, fast, and escape modules based on patterns of recruitment and phasic synaptic drive during fictive swimming (El Manira, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recruitment probability varies based on morphological type, with V2a-D neurons always firing more sparsely than V2a-B neurons, regardless of speed.
source: However, we also find that recruitment probability varies based on morphological type, with V2a-D neurons always firing more sparsely than V2a-B neurons, regardless of speed.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings in this study.

claim: Increases in speed in juveniles/adults and larvae are initially accomplished via more reliable V2a neuron recruitment.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that increases in speed in juveniles/adults and larvae are initially accomplished via more reliable V2a neuron recruitment, as also reported in mice (Zhong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and supported by citation to work in mice.

claim: Relatively low initial forces rely on recruitment of motor neurons.
source: This fits studies of motor neurons, where relatively low initial forces rely on recruitment (Enoka and Duchateau, 2017; Jay et al., 2023), while higher forces are achieved by increasing firing rates (Bhatt et al., 2007; Enoka and Duchateau, 2017), in addition to silencing more easily recruited neurons (Smith et al., 1980; Kyriakatos et al., 2011; Menelaou and McLean, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Higher forces are achieved by increasing firing rates of motor neurons.
source: This fits studies of motor neurons, where relatively low initial forces rely on recruitment (Enoka and Duchateau, 2017; Jay et al., 2023), while higher forces are achieved by increasing firing rates (Bhatt et al., 2007; Enoka and Duchateau, 2017), in addition to silencing more easily recruited neurons (Smith et al., 1980; Kyriakatos et al., 2011; Menelaou and McLean, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A common mechanism of rhythmogenesis is insufficient to explain the full operational range of locomotion.
source: In sum, our findings suggest that cell-type-specific modes of spinal rhythmogenesis are responsible for different speeds, which means a common mechanism of rhythmogenesis is insufficient to explain the full operational range of locomotion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the Discussion.
